claims.text: Valence electron concentration per atom governs superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Valence electron concentration influences the density of states at the Fermi level.
Substituting elements with different valences systematically varies valence electron concentration per atom.
Local atomic arrangement and the resulting electronic structure mediate the effect of the intervention.
The density of states at the Fermi level influences the superconducting transition temperature.
Superconducting transition temperature will correlate with valence electron concentration per atom.
Higher valence electron concentrations will produce higher superconducting transition temperatures.
The proposed material remains a solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
A failure to find a correlation between valence electron concentration and superconducting transition temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Elemental substitution necessarily changes chemical composition, whereas the conditions require constant solid-solution composition. The intended controlled variable may be phase constitution or all non-substituted composition variables, but that is not stated.

Temperature is stated to be constant, but determining a superconducting transition temperature ordinarily requires a temperature-dependent measurement. The condition may mean otherwise identical temperature protocols, but it is written inconsistently.
